searches.note: Thirty three searches of a share of sixty; twenty seven are left unspent. One shared search (the Grosser Ring of 1908 and its auction) serves Egon Müller and Thanisch. Three returned nothing of use on their question: one on the Scharzhof restricted to the estate's domain (only its contact page came back), one on Thanisch that drifted to King Edward VII, and one on the meaning of the Grünhaus names; a fourth on Johann Josef Prüm's dates found only the one source already read. Eleven were restricted to a primary body's or a house's own domain (vdp.de five times, drloosen.de twice, maximingruenhaus.de twice, scharzhof.de and thanisch.com) and are read as primary through their summaries. One WebFetch was tried, on glossary.wein.plus, refused by the network and never retried. The checked blocks carry by: refuter, the only value schema.cjs accepts, though this run was asked to sign as researcher.

method: The fragment was written with no web search at all, resting on the Codex's library and region records and on the writer's memory; this recheck searched every fact beyond the Codex, the strongest first: the founders and the dates, the classification and the auction, the sites and their soils, the making and its vessels, the label words and every beat of the story.

A fact the Codex states (the Prädikat floors, the region's name to 2007, the Ortsteil, the Grosslage traps, the Mosel's sundials, the law of 1971) stands on the Codex; every other fact now rests on a house's own page, the VDP's or two secondary sources, or is taken out.

Sources whose address carries a writer's name (a Mosel writer's blog on the Scharzhof, a wine wiki under a first name, an importer's site under a person's name) were read in the results but never cited.

tested: The year 1797: Primum Familiae Vini has a great great grandfather of the family acquiring the Scharzhof in 1797; wein.plus has the estate auctioned in 1797 after the secularisation; a Trier University lecture and a writer's blog (not cited) give the auction of July 1797 and the buyer as Jakob or Jacques Koch: confirmed, told as an auction bought by a forebear.

The passing to the Müllers: wein.plus alone has a part of the estate coming to Felix Müller (1810 to 1888) by marriage in 1837 and the whole under his son Egon Müller I (1853 to 1932): one source, so the record says only that the forebear's descendants, the Müllers among them, kept it.
The monastery of Trier: wein.plus and a merchant's wiki give the convent of St Marien at Trier from about 700; the record keeps a monastery of Trier, unnamed.

Ungrafted vines: Falstaff (about a third of the family's part, with the head of the house quoted), Westgarth and Wanderlust (vines planted in the late nineteenth century): confirmed, the hectares left out as volatile.

The making: Westgarth has fermentation in thousand litre oak Fuder casks in deep natural cellars by wild yeasts, slow and gentle; the Sommelier Academy has the wines fermented and raised in Fuder save the TBA; one page has the fermentation stopped with sulphur: corrected to wild yeasts in old Fuder and a stopped fermentation, the cellar's cold, the lees through winter and the spring bottling cut.

The Grosser Ring: founded at Trier in 1908 by the VDP's Mosel page and wein.plus; the auction was held in November 2025 by the VDP's calendar and moves to the spring by wein.plus's magazine: confirmed, September cut as volatile.
Le Gallais and the Braune Kupp: the VDP lists the Le Gallais estate under the family and the Braune Kupp as a Grosse Lage of Wiltingen: confirmed as the library has it.

The rules: nobody living named (the head of the house is described), no price (the library's costliest white left out), no score, nothing volatile (the hectares, the share of the hill and the auction's month left out), no judging superlative (rarest cut from the story), British, no dash; the questions have one key, options of one kind and an explanation naming the nearest wrong option; the first card's one letter away was untrue and is corrected: sound.

changed.was: Through the Middle Ages the Scharzhof and its hill belonged to a monastery of Trier, and the slope above the house was planted with vines for centuries before any Müller lived there. When the French, who then held the left bank of the Rhine, took church property and sold it, the estate changed hands, and in 1797, by the house's account, it passed to the family whose descendants have kept it. Several heads of the house in the generations that followed carried the name Egon, so the label names a line rather than one man. Germany's wine law of 1971 fixed the Prädikat ladder of Kabinett, Spätlese and Auslese that the labels follow, and the Saar became part of a region simply called Mosel in 2007. Through those changes the estate held to sweet wine of very low alcohol and very high acid, picking the hill in several passes so that each Prädikat is a true selection. Its rarer Auslesen and Trockenbeerenauslesen go to the September auction of the Grosser Ring at Trier, the association of the Mosel's auction estates founded in 1908. A candidate who knows the Spätlese knows the Saar's measure, the hill and the hand of the auction wines in a frame a table can share.
changed.now: Through the Middle Ages the Scharzhof and its hill belonged to a monastery of Trier, and the slope was planted with vines long before any Müller lived there. When the French, who then held the land, took church property and sold it, the estate went to auction in 1797, and a forebear of the family bought it; his descendants, the Müllers among them, have kept it since. Several heads of the house carried the name Egon, so the label names a line rather than one man. Germany's wine law of 1971 fixed the Prädikat ladder of Kabinett, Spätlese and Auslese that the labels follow, and in 2007 the region's name, Mosel-Saar-Ruwer, was shortened to Mosel. Through those changes the estate held to sweet wine of very low alcohol and very high acid, fermented with wild yeasts in Fuder casks and picked in several passes so that each Prädikat is a true selection. Lots of its Auslese and Trockenbeerenauslese are sold at the Trier auction of the Grosser Ring, the association of the Mosel's auction estates founded there in 1908. A candidate who knows the Spätlese knows the Saar's measure, the hill and the hand of the auction wines in a frame a table can share.
changed.why: The auction of 1797 and the forebear's purchase by Primum Familiae Vini and wein.plus; the region renamed in 2007, the Saar not joining it then; the auction's month is volatile (November 2025, the spring from 2027); rarest is a rank.

tested: The founding of 1911: Wikipedia has the estate founded in 1911 by Johann Josef Prüm after a division of the original estate, by one account among seven heirs; wein.plus and Falstaff have the division of 1911 too: confirmed, the founder now one of the heirs rather than a son.
The founder's dates (1873 to 1944): found in one source only, and a search on them found nothing more: he stays described.

The son: Wikipedia has him at the estate from 1920; another account has him taking over in 1920; Decanter's profile and others have him dead in 1969 and his sons taking over; one source has him forging the style in the 1930s and 1940s and another dates the estate's fame from his time: confirmed, told as credited with the style.

The sundial: 1842 by the Codex's w-wehlener-sonnenuhr and by wein.plus, which names Jodocus Prüm (1807 to 1876) and has him building dials at Wehlen and Zeltingen; his dates are in one source only, so he stays described; the dial's purpose for the workers was found nowhere and is cut.

The making: Decanter and CellarTracker give spontaneous fermentation, cool, mostly in stainless steel with long lees, CellarTracker a small share of wooden casks as the year decides; one source has the fermentation stopped by cooling and sulphur: added.

The capsules: two merchants give the Goldkapsel and the long Goldkapsel as richer, more botrytised Auslese lots, the long one also on BA, TBA and Eiswein: confirmed; the old link to the law of 1971 is not claimed.

S.A. Prüm: Wikipedia has Joh. Jos. born of the division of the original S.A. Prüm estate and wein.plus and Winetourism have S.A. Prüm founded in 1911 from the family's vineyards: the library's unrelated is wrong, and the record says only that several Prüm estates share the name.

The rules: the living family (the founder's grandsons and great granddaughter) not named; no price; no score (critics' marks met in results, none carried); the Kabinett's hardest to make well, a judgement, replaced; British; no dash; questions sound: sound.

changed.was: The sundial that names the Sonnenuhr was set in the slate across the river from Wehlen in 1842 by a member of the Prüm family, so that the people working the steep slope could tell the time. The family's holdings were divided among heirs in 1911, and the son who took his share founded the estate whose label carries his name in short. His own son ran it from the 1920s to the 1960s and gave it the style it is known by: picking late, fermenting with the cellar's own yeasts and stopping with natural sugar, so that the young wines smell of struck match and seem closed for years. Germany's wine law of 1971 set the Prädikat names on the labels, and the house used the colour of the capsule to mark finer selections within them, a gold capsule for a richer Auslese and a long gold capsule richer again. Other Prüm estates share the name and the village, which keeps guests and candidates alert. The estate's fame rests on sweet wines that a patient cellar turns into honey and smoke over decades. Two habits come with it: read the village before the vineyard, and look at the capsule as well as the print.
changed.now: The sundial that names the Sonnenuhr was set in the slate across the river from Wehlen in 1842 by a member of the Prüm family. In 1911 the family estate was divided among heirs, and one of them founded the estate whose label carries his name in short. His son worked there from 1920 and led it until his death in 1969, and he is credited with the style it is known by: light, sweet wines, fermented with wild yeasts and stopped with natural sugar, that smell of struck match when young and seem closed for years. Germany's wine law of 1971 set the Prädikat names on the labels; within them the house marks a richer Auslese with a gold capsule and a richer one again with a long gold capsule. Other Prüm estates share the name and the village, which keeps guests and candidates alert. The estate's fame rests on sweet wines that a patient cellar turns into honey and smoke over decades. Two habits come with it: read the village before the vineyard, and look at the capsule as well as the print.
changed.why: Wikipedia, wein.plus and Falstaff have one of the heirs of 1911 founding the estate; the son's years from Wikipedia and Decanter; the dial's purpose found nowhere; the style told as the wine, not as late picking, which no source gives.

tested: The family's two centuries and 1988: the estate's About us page has the family for over two hundred years and the son leading it since 1988: confirmed; the VDP from 1993 by the same page: added.
Ungrafted old vines: the estate has every parcel on its own roots; the VDP's estate page has vines up to 120 years old in the Prälat: confirmed, a century old added.

The Prälat: the VDP's page has a steep, rocky site across from the village of Erden, red slate, marked out of the Treppchen at the end of the nineteenth century and named in honour of Prof. Dr. Franz Steffens (1853 to 1930), a grower's son from Ürzig; the estate has a warm microclimate, a south facing slope and red slate, sheltered between river and rock: the amphitheatre between the cliffs, the rock storing the sun and the water reflecting it, and a churchman who once held it were corrected or cut; counted the warmest of the Mittelmosel stays as the Codex's, the estate's exceptionally warm supporting it.

The making: the estate has spontaneous fermentation in wooden barrels, lees ageing of twelve or twenty four months and no stirring; Best of Wines has spontaneous fermentation in large neutral casks for every single vineyard wine and about twelve months on the lees for the sweet Prädikat wines; one source has some steel, contradicting the estate: corrected to large old oak casks and about a year on unstirred lees; picked late cut.
Eroica: the first vintage 1999, with Chateau Ste. Michelle, by Ste. Michelle's own page and Decanter: confirmed.
The Pfalz: the library's own fact; its year (1996 in the writer's memory) found nowhere and left out.

The Würzgarten: the estate calls it Rotliegend rock of volcanic origin, the VDP weathered red slate debris rich in iron oxide: the others and the trap now say iron rich Rotliegend of volcanic origin mixed with slate; across the river from Erden was wrong for Ürzig's slope and is gone.

The rules: the son is living and is not named (he and his name in the library are listed below); no price; no score (a critic's list met in results, not carried); nothing volatile (hectares left out); no judging superlative; British; no dash; the new story question has four options of one kind, the nearest wrong option (the Doctor's archbishop) named in the explanation: sound.

changed.was: Around Bernkastel the Loosens have owned vines for some two centuries, by the family's own account, and over that time they gathered parcels in the great slopes downriver: the Würzgarten at Ürzig and the Treppchen and the Prälat at Erden. The Prälat takes its name from a prelate, a churchman who once held it, and its red slate between cliffs and water makes it the warm heart of that stretch of the river. Many of the family's vines there grow on their own roots, phylloxera having been ill at home in the dry slate. In 1988 a son of the family took over the estate and set it on a new course: lower yields, long ageing in the old Fuder casks of the cellar, and a campaign to carry Mosel Riesling back onto the wine lists of the world. That work took the estate beyond the valley. In 1999 it made the first Eroica Riesling with Chateau Ste. Michelle of Washington State, and it also took on an estate in the Pfalz. The Prälat Auslese stayed at the centre of the range as the estate's most concentrated wine. Set beside a Wehlen wine, it shows the other face of the slate, red rock and warmth, orange and ginger where blue slate gives peach and lime.
changed.now: Around Bernkastel the Loosens have owned vines for more than two centuries, by the family's own account, and over that time they gathered parcels in the steep slopes downriver: the Würzgarten at Ürzig and the Treppchen and the Prälat at Erden. The Prälat was part of the Treppchen until it was marked out as a site of its own at the end of the nineteenth century, and it was named in honour of a prelate and professor from Ürzig, a grower's son. Its red slate between rock and water makes it the warm heart of that stretch of the river, and the family's vines there grow on their own roots. In 1988 a son of the family took over the estate and set out to carry Mosel Riesling back onto the wine lists of the world; the estate joined the VDP in 1993. That work took it beyond the valley. In 1999 it made the first Eroica Riesling with Chateau Ste. Michelle of Washington State, and it also took on an estate in the Pfalz. The Prälat Auslese stayed at the centre of the range as its most concentrated wine. Set beside a Wehlen wine, it shows the other face of the slate, red rock and warmth, orange and ginger where blue slate gives peach and lime.

The family: the VDP's portrait of the estate has twelve generations on the Middle Mosel since the first half of the seventeenth century; wein.plus gives 1636; the estate's site claims 385 years: confirmed, at Bernkastel for centuries replaced by the Middle Mosel.
The share of the Doctor: the Codex's region line (since the nineteenth century) and a VDP page (parcels for two hundred years): confirmed; a large share was not found and is cut.

The doctor and the widow: the VDP's portrait has the doctor, a member of the Prussian House of Representatives, dead in 1895 at forty one, his widow twenty nine with three small children and the estate named Witwe Dr. H. Thanisch after her; wein.plus has the Prussian member of parliament as the estate's founder: confirmed and dated.

The Grosser Ring: the VDP's portrait, in the estate's words, has the widow among the founding members of the Grosser Ring and then of the VDP in 1910; the Grosser Ring of 1908 by the VDP and wein.plus: added as the estate's account.
The division of 1988: wein.plus and CellarTracker: confirmed and dated (the writer had left it out).

The Doctor: the VDP gives dark, rocky soil of weathered Devonian slate with much fine earth, blue and grey slate, a gradient to 70 per cent facing south south west, and mostly ungrafted Riesling; Thanisch and Wegeler among its VDP growers: the near vertical slope and the clay and loam corrected.

The label and the making: the estate's site and two merchants (Valckenberg and Corney and Barrow) print Berncasteler Doctor; Valckenberg's sheet has a 2019 Auslese hand picked in several selections, spontaneously fermented and raised in oak, Corney and Barrow a 2008 Spätlese fermented in stainless steel with wild yeasts: the label term and the making are rewritten on them.

The rules: the living family and the owner of the other estate are not named; no price (two auction prices met for a TBA of 1921, not carried; the library's land values left out); nothing volatile (the hectares left out); no judging superlative; British; no dash; the questions sound: sound.

changed.was: The legend of the Doctor is set in 1360: an Archbishop of Trier, lying ill with a fever at the castle above Bernkastel, was brought wine from this slope and recovered, and he named it the true doctor. The vineyard has carried the name since. The Thanisch family, at Bernkastel for centuries by its own account, came to hold a large share of the slope in the nineteenth century. When the head of the family, a doctor by degree, died towards the end of that century, his widow took charge, and her title stayed on the label: Wwe., short for Witwe, before Dr. H. Thanisch. Through the twentieth century the Doctor was shared among only a few owners, and Germany's wine law of 1971 set the Prädikat names, Kabinett, Spätlese and Auslese, that its labels carry. Later the family divided its holdings between heirs, and two estates came to bear the name, Erben Thanisch and Erben Müller-Burggraef, each with its own part of the Doctor. The Spätlese is the house's classic reading of the site: smoky, dense and firm, where Wehlen is lighter and Graach broader. Read the long name to the end, then, since the heirs and not the widow tell you which house made the wine.
changed.now: The legend of the Doctor is set in 1360: an Archbishop of Trier, lying ill with a fever at Landshut castle above Bernkastel, was brought wine from this slope and recovered, and he named it the true doctor. The vineyard has carried the name since. The Thanisch family has grown vines on the Middle Mosel since the first half of the seventeenth century, by its own account, and it came to hold a share of the Doctor in the nineteenth. The head of the family, a doctor by degree and a member of the Prussian parliament, died in 1895 at forty one; his widow took charge with three small children, and her title stayed on the label: Wwe., short for Witwe, before Dr. H. Thanisch. By the estate's account she was among the founders of the Grosser Ring, the Mosel's auction estates, in 1908. In 1988 the family divided its holdings between heirs, and two estates came to bear the name, Erben Thanisch and Erben Müller-Burggraef, each with its own part of the Doctor. The Spätlese is the house's classic reading of the site: smoky, dense and firm. Read the long name to the end, then, since the heirs and not the widow tell you which house made the wine.
changed.why: Landshut castle by the VDP and the town; the family on the Middle Mosel, the doctor's death in 1895 at forty one and the widow by the VDP's portrait and wein.plus; the Grosser Ring as the estate's account; the division of 1988 by wein.plus and CellarTracker.

tested: The year 966: the estate's history pages have a charter of 966 in which the Emperor Otto I confirmed a gift made in the seventh century by the Frankish king Dagobert I to the Benedictine abbey of St Maximin at Trier, the Grünhaus a secondary holding of the abbey: confirmed, told without naming either ruler.

The sale under the French: the estate has it auctioned in 1811 under Napoleon's secularisation, to a Freiherr von Handel, then the von Solemacher family: corrected from the start of the nineteenth century and dated.

The year 1882: the estate's timeline has Carl Ferdinand Freiherr von Stumm-Halberg buying the estate in 1882 and, having no surviving son, giving it to his daughter Ida as her dowry on her marriage to Conrad von Schubert: corrected from bought by the von Schubert family; the family's ownership is counted from 1882 by the estate.

The three hills: the estate has three monopoles named after the old monastic hierarchy; a merchant has the Bruderberg's wine for the monks, the Herrenberg's for the choir lords and the Abtsberg's for the abbots; the estate calls the vineyards contiguous and enclosed, and no source calls them walled: walled cut, the order of rank kept as the Codex's, the lords' kept as the plain translation.
The Abtsberg: the estate gives blue Devonian slate on a rounded summit with slopes to 75 per cent, a steep south facing slope in the Ruwer valley, the upper Herrenberg on red slate: added.

The making: the estate has the Kabinetts fermented only spontaneously and raised in the historic cellar, the musts in thousand litre oak Fuder casks or small steel tanks with wild yeasts, Fuder casks of local oak: added; the vaulted cellar below the house, picking by hand and the spring bottling were not found and are cut.

The rules: the living family (the fifth and sixth generations met in results and a document's title) not named; no price (an auction price of 1923 met, not carried); nothing volatile (the hectares left out); no judging superlative (among the region's most delicate softened to delicate); British; no dash; the story question's distractors now come from the estate's own timeline and the Codex's Rheingau: sound.

changed.was: The Grünhaus first appears in the records in 966, when the Emperor Otto I (912 to 973) confirmed it as a possession of the Benedictine abbey of St Maximin at Trier, and the abbey's monks worked its slopes for some eight centuries. The order of its three walled vineyards follows the abbey's own ranks: the Abtsberg was the abbot's, the Herrenberg the lords', the Bruderberg the brothers'. Under French rule at the start of the nineteenth century the abbey's lands were taken and sold, and in 1882 the estate was bought by the von Schubert family. They kept the three vineyards apart and printed each name under the estate's own, Maximin Grünhäuser, which German law treats as an Ortsteil standing in place of a village. The Ruwer is a small, cool side valley, and its wines are among the region's most delicate, scented with herbs and blackcurrant leaf. When the region's name was shortened to Mosel in 2007, the Ruwer's name left the label, though the valley's style did not. The Abtsberg is the estate's first wine in rank, and its Kabinett is the lightest way to meet it. In three names the estate keeps the order in which an abbey ranked its own hills.
changed.now: The Grünhaus first appears in writing in 966, when an imperial charter confirmed a gift that a Frankish king had made in the seventh century to the Benedictine abbey of St Maximin at Trier, and the abbey's monks worked its slopes for centuries. Its three hills take their names from the abbey's order of rank: the Abtsberg the abbot's, the Herrenberg the lords', the Bruderberg the brothers'. In 1811, under Napoleon's secularisation, the estate was sold at auction to its first lay owner, a baron, and it passed through another family before 1882, when a baron of the Stumm family bought it; his daughter brought it to the von Schubert family as her dowry on her marriage. The three vineyards, each a monopole of the estate, are printed under the estate's own name, Maximin Grünhäuser, which German law treats as an Ortsteil standing in place of a village. The Ruwer is a small, cool side valley, and its wines are delicate, scented with herbs and blackcurrant leaf. The Abtsberg is the estate's first wine in rank, and its Kabinett the lightest way to meet it: in three names the estate keeps the order in which an abbey ranked its own hills.
changed.why: The estate's own timeline gives the charter of 966 and Dagobert's gift, the auction of 1811, the families between and the purchase and dowry of 1882; walled cut; three monopoles.
